finding: §1 describes a release that no longer exists, and §1 is what an implementer decomposes from. It reads: Two deliverables, and only the first is a no-op by default ... §3 changes consecutive_clean and converged for any project whose spec moves between rounds, opted in or not. An earlier draft of this paragraph claimed the whole release was behaviour-preserving; it is not, and §3 is why. §3 is now titled What this release deliberately does not contain and specifies no mechanism at all - the spec-hash reset was cut to spec/0.46.0.md §8.4 (verified present, spec/0.46.0.md:335). So the release has ONE deliverable and IS behaviour-preserving by default, and §1 states the opposite three times in five lines. No test can be written for a second deliverable that has no section, and the claim that the release is not behaviour-preserving now has no observable anywhere in §5.
suggestion: Rewrite the paragraph to one deliverable: §2 ships audit_converge_on and changes nothing for a project that does not set it. If a behaviour-preserving claim is kept, give it the assertion that makes it falsifiable - on a fixture with audit_converge_on unset, tp audit --record and --status emit byte-identical payloads before and after this release.

finding: Test 8 cannot reach its pinned answers through the function tp ships, and the term that blocks it is not the one §3 removed. Measured: engine.Converged (internal/engine/reviewstate.go:509-511) is ConsecutiveClean(rounds) >= requiredCleanRounds && !StateStale(rounds, currentHash). The staleness term is pre-existing and untouched by this release. Test 8 copies the rows of v0.35.0 nine recorded rounds and v0.36.0 thirteen into testdata; those rounds carry the spec_hash of those specs, which cannot equal the hash of whatever spec the test fixture uses, so StateStale is true and every replayed answer is converged false under both policies - blocking at 3 and all at 9 are unreachable. The draft cut in round 5 carried a fixture clause pinning exactly this (the last round spec_hash equals the current spec hash) and it was deleted with §3, but the term it defended against belongs to Converged, not to the reset. So the cut removed a guard whose subject survived the cut.
suggestion: State in test 8 either that the replay calls the clean and streak arithmetic directly rather than Converged, or that the copied rounds carry the fixture spec hash so StateStale is false. Add the negative control that keeps it honest: the same fixture with a foreign hash on the last round reports converged false under both policies, so a test that passes for the staleness reason is distinguishable from one that passes for the policy reason.

finding: The documentation sweep §2 puts in scope is already done, so the scope claim is false and no acceptance written from it can fail. §2 says the five-layer chain still stands in two other places this release must sweep - skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:519-522 states it as the rule for workflow fields, and spec/0.31.0.md:41 carries it for the twin - and that REFERENCE.md:327-328 additionally names TP_RUN_MAX_UNITS and TP_REVIEW_MAX_ROUNDS. Measured, all three are already correct. REFERENCE.md:521-522 reads Resolution (resolve-at-read) ... The chain differs by field kind, and conflating them has cost two specs a review round each, and the code block at :524 reads workflow fields task-file workflow override > .tp/config.json > built-in default - the correct three layers; the cited range 519-522 contains no chain at all. spec/0.31.0.md:41 reads task override > project config > built-in default with the parenthetical this sentence read CLI > env > ... until v0.37.0 review round 5. REFERENCE.md:328-330 names the two variables only inside a parenthetical that states neither exists in any non-test source. A unit given this paragraph as acceptance finds nothing to change, or edits already-correct text.
suggestion: Delete the sweep sentence, or restate it as an invariant a guard can check and fail: no line in spec/*.md, skills/tp/REFERENCE.md or skills/tp/SKILL.md states a CLI or environment layer for a workflow field. That form can go red; the current form cannot. Keep the verified fact that a scoped search for TP_REVIEW_CONVERGE_ON under internal/ returns zero - that one is exact.

finding: Test 9 pins both write paths and not the direction, and the fence tp already ships is directional, so two engineers build opposite fences and both pass. Test 9 asserts only audit_converge_on=blocking - exit 2 under TP_UNATTENDED=1, exit 0 without - and never says what tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=all does under TP_UNATTENDED=1. The precedent makes this a real choice rather than an omission: REFERENCE.md:323-326 states an equal or lower value is accepted and exits 0, since lowering a budget cannot manufacture convergence, and fenceWorkflowWrite (internal/cli/unattended.go:69) refuses only when engine.UnattendedRaise reports a raise. One engineer fences every write to the field; the other fences only the relaxing direction and lets a unit tighten to all. Both are green on test 9, and the difference is observable: under the blanket reading a unit cannot restore the strict default it was told to restore.
suggestion: State the rule in §2 and give test 9 its second arm. Either audit_converge_on=all also exits 2 under TP_UNATTENDED=1 because the field is human-only in both directions, or it exits 0 because tightening cannot manufacture convergence, mirroring the cap rule. Assert the chosen one and its opposite as the failing arm, on both write paths.

finding: §2 says the fence does not fit a string field and then costs the widening as two new call sites, and the two statements cannot both be acted on. fenceWorkflowWrite(field string, requested float64) is numeric through its whole body, not only in its signature (internal/cli/unattended.go:56-82): engine.FencedCapField gates entry and returns silently at :64-66 for an unfenced field, engine.ResolvedCapValue returns a float, engine.UnattendedRaise is a numeric comparison, and refuseUnattended composes the message setting %s to %s above the resolved %s through formatCapValue. A string field routed through that path either produces no refusal at all or produces the message setting audit_converge_on to blocking above the resolved all. So the release needs a new membership predicate and a new message, not two call sites - and §5 pins neither, because test 9 asserts exit codes only and is green over a refusal whose hint says above the resolved.
suggestion: Cost it as what it is: a string-valued fence helper beside fenceWorkflowWrite, a membership predicate in place of UnattendedRaise, and a refusal message with no comparison in it. Then extend test 9 past the exit code - the refusal hint on both paths names tp escalate --decision audit-converge-on and contains no comparison word - which is also the assertion that catches the reuse of the cap message.

finding: The normative table in §2 and test 7 give opposite answers for a non-PASS row carrying no severity, which is the case tp own shipped fixtures produce. The table defines blocking as: no non-PASS row in the round carries a blocking severity. A row with severity null, or with no severity key, carries no severity at all, so under the table it does not carry a blocking one and the round is clean. The fail-closed sentence covers an unrecognised severity, and §2 itself establishes that null is not an unrecognised value but tp own marker for not applicable - every one of 2,913 PASS rows carries severity: null. Test 7 then pins (b) null and (c) absent as blocking. Two engineers reading §2 alone write opposite predicates. The case is not hypothetical: signalRow (internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:40-42) emits {item_id, role, status} with no severity key, so the rows in the release own reversed guard are all case (c), and §4 depends on them counting as blocking.
suggestion: Replace the table row with the three-way rule the tests need: under blocking a round is clean when every non-PASS row carries a severity that is present, recognised and non-blocking - so error, an out-of-enum value, null and an absent key all block, and only warning and info do not. Then §2, test 7 and §4 state one predicate instead of three.

finding: Three cross-references in §4 point at a §3 and a test that do not exist after this round rewrite, and one of them is the only pin §4 claims on nine assertions. (1) Non-Goal 2 keeps the first two true; §5 test 12 pins all nine - §5 has eleven items; the pin is test 11. (2) assert.Len(t, e, 3, ...) which §3 reset touches - §3 contains no reset; it is now the section recording that the reset was cut, so nothing in this release touches :498. (3) Non-Goal 4: §3 adds a function rather than altering the shared one precisely so review --status cannot move - §3 adds no function, so the mechanism Non-Goal 4 names as its own protection is gone and nothing in §5 asserts that review --status is unmoved. All three read as live requirements and none resolves; a unit reading (1) looks for a twelfth test and finds eleven.
suggestion: Renumber test 12 to test 11; delete the §3-reset clause from the :498 sentence, since no part of this release now touches that assertion; and rewrite Non-Goal 4 as what is now true - this release adds no code on the review path at all - then give it the observable that makes it checkable, that review --status output is unchanged with audit_converge_on set to either value.

finding: The §2.2 closing sentence points the implementer at the wrong test after the §5 renumbering. It reads: §5 test 5 uses a legacy row because it is convenient and real, not because the case is live. Test 5 is now warning is advisory and names no legacy row; the legacy fixture is test 7 case (a), whose own text reads a legacy row supplies only (a): all 67 carry a present, non-null high/medium/low. A reader following §2.2 to test 5 finds a test about warning severity and no legacy fixture at all, so the sentence justifying the fixture choice attaches to nothing and the fixture it justifies is left unexplained.
suggestion: Point it at test 7(a). While renumbering, make the reference mutual - test 7(a) is the only §5 item §2.2 governs, so naming each other in both directions makes the next renumbering break loudly rather than silently.

finding: The dependency §4 states for its nine surviving assertions is over-broad by eight, which makes test 11 read as a fail-closed test when only one of its assertions is one. §4: those nine hold only because signalRow (audit_signal_test.go:40-42) emits no severity key, so §2 fail-closed rule keeps the round unclean. Measured against the test body (internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:469-503): :481 and :484 are exit-code requires on --resolve and --record; :485-487 asserts role_streaks {go-safety, consecutive_clean 0, open 1}, which §2 itself says is computed through AuditRowIsPass alone and is severity-blind; and :493, :494, :497, :498, :500 all read the payload recorded by divergingFixture BEFORE line 472 sets anything, so no policy applies to them. Exactly one assertion depends on the fail-closed rule - :490, the --check exit 1. Stating it over all nine tells an implementer that eight assertions need protection they do not need, and hides the fact that the one dependent assertion duplicates test 7(c), so a broken fail-closed rule reddens test 7(c) and test 11 together and neither localises it.
suggestion: Attribute the dependency to :490 alone, and say in test 11 that its failure is expected to accompany test 7(c) rather than to localise anything. Also write down which fixture test 11 runs under: keeping the line-472 write leaves the nine executing under blocking, deleting it keeps them at the default, both pass, so the choice cannot be discovered from the test and must be stated.

finding: §5 opens with a quantifier over its own list that the list falsifies, and it is the sentence certifying the list is safe to build from. Every test names the input that makes it fail. Counted against the eleven items: test 1 names one (an implementation shipping blocking as the built-in), test 2 names one (a resolver reading only the project layer) and test 9 names one (an implementation that fences one file). The remaining eight - 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11 - name none; what 5, 7, 8 and 11 add is a reason the fixture was chosen, which is not a failing input. So the certifying sentence is true of three of eleven, and it is the sentence that would otherwise catch the two tests in this list that cannot fail as written (test 3 and test 10, filed separately).
suggestion: Either add the failing input to the eight, or replace the quantifier with the count the list supports - three of these tests name the mutation that kills them, the rest name an expected observable. The repository rule is that a quantifier over an unenumerated set is the sentence that rots; here it rotted within one round of the list being rewritten, which is the argument for the count rather than the claim.

finding: Test 3 names the two surfaces and no expected value on either, so it cannot be written the same way twice. tp config --extract emits the field - with its resolved value, with its source, or as a key copied out of a task-file override? tp validate --project accepts and rejects it - accepts which values, rejects what, and at which exit code? The exit code is already load-bearing in the twin and the two cases differ: spec/0.31.0.md:41 splits exit 2 (a literal command-line argument being persisted) from exit 1 (a stored layer a consuming command resolves), and tp validate --project reads a stored layer, so its refusal is the exit-1 path while test 2 refusal is the exit-2 path. Nothing in test 3 says so. The round-5 finding this test answers named the values explicitly; the repair adopted the surfaces and dropped them.
suggestion: Pin them: tp config --extract emits audit_converge_on with its resolved value and its source; tp validate --project exits 0 on all and on blocking and exits 1 on a third value with the same hint shape engine.ReviewConvergeOnHint uses. Say that this exit code is 1 and test 2 is 2, since that difference is the part of the v0.31.0 defect most likely to be re-made.

finding: Test 10 asserts an observable tp has nowhere: A fenced refusal records --decision audit-converge-on, not other. Measured, a fenced refusal records nothing. refuseUnattended (internal/cli/unattended.go:33-38) prints an error plus the hint escalate instead: tp escalate --decision <name> --evidence <what you found> and exits 2; the record at $TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-escalation.json is written only when a unit later runs tp escalate, a separate command whose --decision is enforced by IsEscalationDecision (escalate.go:41). So records is true of neither surface at the moment of the refusal, and three non-equivalent assertions fit the sentence: the refusal hint text contains --decision audit-converge-on; escalationDecision(audit_converge_on) returns audit-converge-on rather than other; or tp escalate --decision audit-converge-on is accepted instead of being a usage error. An implementation can satisfy the third and fail the first, which is the likely partial - adding the enum entry without extending escalationDecision leaves every refusal hint still saying other.
suggestion: Name the surface and take the pair that catches that partial: the refusal hint on both fenced write paths contains tp escalate --decision audit-converge-on, and tp escalate --decision audit-converge-on inside a run writes decision audit-converge-on into the escalation record. State the killing mutation as the enum entry added without escalationDecision being extended.

finding: §2 bans a word one line after its own normative table uses it, and the table is the artifact an implementer implements. The table row for all reads no non-PASS row survives, whatever its severity. The very next paragraph reads: Surviving is deliberately not the word: it would imply a disposition that removes a row from the count, which Non-Goal 2 declines to create. The correction is right and the artifact it corrects was not changed, so the release ships a normative predicate written in the word the release says is wrong - and the same word carries into §5 test 4 (a round with one surviving info row), Non-Goal 6 (surviving warning and info rows) and, in an unrelated sense, test 11 (the nine surviving assertions). An implementer reading the table alone builds the disposition-aware predicate Non-Goal 2 declines, and test 4 wording does not catch it because the fixture has nothing disposed.
suggestion: Rewrite both table rows without the word - all: the round has no non-PASS row; blocking: no non-PASS row in the round carries a blocking severity - and fix test 4 and Non-Goal 6 in the same pass. The explaining paragraph can then go, since nothing is left to correct.

finding: The repaired count in Non-Goal 6 is right and one of its four citations is not, in the sentence whose whole subject is a count copied before anyone checked it. Four places pin the absence of nonblocking_open on the audit side by name: spec/0.31.0.md §8.4 and its test 18, skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:634, and reviewconvergeon_clean_test.go:185-205. Three verify - spec/0.31.0.md:100 and :141 carry the pin, and reviewconvergeon_clean_test.go:185-205 is exactly TestReviewNonBlockingOpen_AuditUnaffected with its two absent assertions. REFERENCE.md:634 does not: that line is inside the --role emission rules (An empty prompts[] gets an empty key). The pin is REFERENCE.md:641, the --compact disposition line naming nonblocking_open (review-only, emitted only on an accepted-open clean round). Off by seven. §4 also records that spec/0.46.0.md still carries the false six (verified at spec/0.46.0.md:330) and assigns no owner for correcting it.
suggestion: Change :634 to :641. Either add the spec/0.46.0.md:330 correction to this release documentation work or state that 0.46.0 corrects its own count, so the known-false number has an owner rather than a footnote.

finding: The last sentence of test 2 is not writable as an assertion: It asserts no CLI or environment layer, because none exists. Neither a flag nor a variable is named, so there is nothing to invoke. An engineer who writes nothing satisfies it. An engineer who writes tp set --audit-converge-on=blocking exits 2 writes a test that passes for every unknown flag and would keep passing if the flag were later added under a different spelling. An engineer who writes with TP_AUDIT_CONVERGE_ON set and no task or project layer the resolved value is still all writes the only version with a failing arm, and nothing in §5 says that is the intended one.
suggestion: Delete the sentence - §2 already states the chain is two layers over the default and the scoped search that supports it - or make it the third version explicitly, naming the variable so the assertion has something to set.

finding: Near-miss twice, both the same reflex - reading a citation as a claim about the world rather than a claim about the cited lines. (1) I set out to falsify the §2 cost figure (16 production .go files, 11 test files) as an instance of this repository known uncounted-quantifier class, and it is exact. The union of ReviewConvergeOn and review_converge_on under internal/ is 16 non-test files - engine/reviewconvergeon.go, engine/configresolve.go, engine/reviewclean.go, engine/projectconfig.go, model/projectconfig.go, model/workflow.go, cli/review.go, cli/review_status.go, cli/review_record.go, cli/set.go, cli/set_project.go, cli/validate_project.go, cli/config_extract.go, cli/config.go, cli/import_enforce.go, cli/budget.go - and 11 test files. It should not be re-challenged in a later round. (2) I nearly let the §2 sweep sentence stand because it cites a line range and reads plausibly; opening REFERENCE.md:519-525 showed the cited range holds no chain at all and the chain seven lines later is already correct, which became this round §2 finding. The general form: a plausible citation is the cheapest thing in a spec to leave unchecked and the most expensive to leave wrong, and a heavily repaired spec is where stale citations concentrate, because a repair moves text and leaves the numbers where they were.
suggestion: No action beyond the rows filed. For the loop: after any round that renumbers a list or retitles a section, sweep every §n and test-n reference in the file before reviewing content - this round produced four such breaks (§1, §2.2, and §4 twice) among fourteen findings, and each of them reads as a live requirement.
